title: FOURTH REPORT: Former Alpha School students speak out
author: Benjamin Riley
summary: In the fourth installment of his investigation into Alpha School, Benjamin Riley turns from adult sources to former students who attended from fall 2022 onward, quoting them on background across several campuses. The students describe a culture they repeatedly call dystopian, with offshore staff monitoring them through webcams and software that flagged eye movements and so-called anti-patterns, which Riley sets against MacKenzie Price's own public description of the system. He documents a tiered motivation structure, the privileged Rocket Ship and the previously undisclosed Pirate Ship and Omega groups, where students say they were demoted grade levels, segregated during club time and, in one account, had credits manipulated so they could not easily leave. Students also describe being locked out of their computers, or nuked, when accuracy targets were missed, and say they read no complete books. Riley links the monitoring to consultant Carl Hendrick's predictions about AI surveillance, raises open questions about child labor and liability, and notes that Alpha School and the Class Disrupted hosts did not respond. His brief commentary concludes that Alpha's public narrative has been shattered.
points: Former students describe offshore staff watching them through mandatory webcams and software that flagged looking away from the screen as an anti-pattern.
Riley reports two unpublicized tracks, the Pirate Ship and Omega, where lower-performing students say they were demoted and isolated from peers.
Students say missing accuracy targets could get them nuked, locking their computers to the learning app until offsite staff intervened.
Asked whether they read books at Alpha, students said they read passages in the app but not whole books.
Riley raises whether students functioned as unpaid software testers and suggests possible hidden attrition behind Alpha's top-line metrics.
quotes: They hired this data team of people that didn’t live in the U.S. and they would watch us through our computers and it felt really sketchy and scary. It felt like it was more of a science experiment, and I was more of a lab rat rather than [having] someone that actually cared about my learning.
Anti-patterns were like this AI system that decided whether or not you were doing good enough. It saw that your eyes were moving away from the screen, you’ll get flagged for those.

Whether students at Alpha School should be considered part of the company’s software product development team is an open question, and so too is whether this raises issues of child labor law violations or other forms of civil liability.
Based on what my student sources told me, it appears the future Hendrick describes is already present at Alpha School, at least to some degree.
Basically it would shut down your entire computer [other than the 2-Hour Learning app], and just show a jokey screen of a mushroom cloud. “You’ve been nuked.
We never had a curriculum of books to read. Never a full book, only passages [on the software app].
He’s not disclosing to students that when they enter into Alpha, that it is an experiment. He’s saying this is a school and it’s going to work. It’s not a school and it’s not guaranteed to work.
Alpha School’s public narrative has been shattered irreparably. And I will not rest until the full magnitude of its pedagogical and psychological malpractice against children is revealed.
